 Pinned Updated   Oct. 28, 2026, 7:56 p.m. ET Lisa Lerer 
 Here’s the latest. 
 President Trump and former President Barack Obama were both on the campaign trail on Wednesday, holding dueling rallies in states with competitive races for Senate and governor.
 Mr. Obama was in Georgia supporting Senator Jon Ossoff, the Democratic incumbent whose race appears to have shifted to safer ground, and Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, who is in a competitive race for governor against Rick Jackson, a Republican billionaire. In Ohio, Mr. Trump was backing Senator Jon Husted, who is trying to fend off a Democrat seeking a return to the Senate, and Vivek Ramaswamy, whose campaign for governor has faced broad criticism over an attack ad aimed at his opponent.
 Former Vice President Kamala Harris is also scheduled to appear in Georgia, where she will begin a three-day campaign swing with Mr. Ossoff starting on Thursday. Democrats have scaled back their spending on the race in a sign of confidence. But the governor’s contest remains far more competitive, raising the prospect that many voters may split their ticket. 
 Mr. Trump, who has frequently visited conservative strongholds in recent weeks as traditionally Republican-leaning states have turned into political battlegrounds, has already stumped for Mr. Husted twice this month. Mr. Husted is in a close race with former Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat who was ousted by Bernie Moreno two years ago.
 The president has also fiercely defended Mr. Ramaswamy, whose campaign last week aired an ad featuring the estranged mother of his opponent, Dr. Amy Acton. A former state health official, Dr. Acton has said that she has not spoken to her mother since she was removed from her mother’s custody after her stepfather was arrested and charged with raping her.
 Mr. Trump’s sinking approval ratings have expanded the competitive Senate map and forced Republicans to play defense in deep-red states. A new set of New York Times/Siena University polls released on Wednesday shows the Senate contest in South Carolina effectively tied, with Senator Darline Graham, the Republican appointed to her late brother’s seat, leading Dr. Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee, by less than a single percentage point. Republicans are ahead in the Florida Senate race, but by six points, a relatively small margin in a state that Republicans won by double digits just two years ago.
 Here’s what else to know.
 Alaska’s stacked ballot: Operatives aligned with Mary Peltola, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Alaska, spent months recruiting candidates to peel votes from Senator Dan S. Sullivan, the Republican incumbent, The New York Times found. Read more › 
 Talarico the teacher: Years before James Talarico was the Democratic nominee for the U.S. Senate in Texas, he was a sixth-grade English teacher in San Antonio. Former students and teachers at the school said in interviews that they initially feared he’d be in over his head, but he quickly ingratiated himself. Read more › 
 Hard to reach : In a competitive House district in Pennsylvania, residents get their election news from under-the-radar sources — or no sources at all. Read more › 
 Looking to 2028: Several Democrats eyeing the White House have insisted they have been focused on the midterm elections, while stealthily preparing for an extravagantly expensive presidential campaign. Soon, they’ll finally be able to be honest. Read more ›

The event has been a highly polished affair, with a performance from the pop star Janelle Monáe. The crowd also heard from former Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms of Atlanta, the Democratic nominee for governor. Tonight’s event is a clear effort by Ossoff, who has had a commanding lead in the polls against Representative Mike Collins, the Republican Senate nominee, to try to lift up Lance Bottoms, who is in a much tighter race against Rick Jackson, the Republican nominee for governor.

 Reporting from Ohio Though the Trump administration’s attempts to change mail voting rules were unsuccessful, there is a new rule for mail voting in Ohio this year. Absentee ballots that arrive after 7:30 p.m. on Election Day will not be counted, a change pushed by Ohio Republicans last year. As of Wednesday evening, the Ohio secretary of state’s Election Dashboard showed nearly 30 percent of absentee ballots requested in the state had yet to be returned.
 Stephen David, the state’s director for All Voting Is Local, a group working with a nonpartisan election law hotline, said it appeared mail-in voting was running smoothly in Ohio. But his group is recommending that anyone who has not yet put their ballot in the mail now deliver it in person to a dropbox in their county.

 The system to report campaign donations is restored after a hacking attempt. 
 Image The Federal Election Commission outage limited reporting of campaign spending in the final week before the midterms. Credit... Nicole Craine for The New York Times The Federal Election Commission said on Wednesday evening that the agency had restored its electronic filing system, two days after a hacking attempt left candidates, parties and political action committees unable to report campaign donations and spending during a historically expensive advertising cycle.
 The agency switched off its web services late Monday because a “bad actor” was attempting to breach its systems, according to an email sent by an F.E.C. official that was obtained by The New York Times. The hack was reported earlier by Reuters .
 The system remained down into Wednesday. The F.E.C. reported about 5 p.m. Eastern time that it was running again. An F.E.C. spokesman confirmed the outage but declined to say whether a cyberattack had caused the problem. 
 The outage left the public uninformed about spending in federal races less than a week before Election Day, a time when advertising expenditures typically accelerate before voters go to the polls.
 “It’s a serious problem that this information is not being made available to voters right now” while early voting is underway in some states, said Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonpartisan government watchdog. “Voters are going to vote without the full picture that the law entitles them to.”
 In the 20-day window before an election, House and Senate candidates must report donations of $1,000 or more within 48 hours of receiving them, under federal law. PACs and other groups must report certain expenditures of $1,000 or more within 24 hours after they are publicly disseminated.
 Filings can be made by paper, but once committees reach thresholds of financial activity, as they often do, they must file everything electronically.
 Super PACs and other groups reported a daily average of about $80 million in spending over the last two weeks, according to Brendan Glavin, research director at OpenSecrets, a nonpartisan campaign watchdog group. But spending can fluctuate widely day to day. It surpassed $260 million on Oct. 21 alone, he said.
 Myles Martin, an F.E.C. spokesman, pointed to an incident report that said the agency had begun investigating the issue at about 9:30 p.m. on Monday. The report said the agency started putting a fix into place late Tuesday.
 The outage did not affect the F.E.C.’s main website, meaning that users could still find information about prior campaign donations, receipts and political action committees — data that could indicate what a candidate might stand for.
 But it disrupted disclosures in the final days of what has become the most expensive political advertising cycle ever, according to AdImpact, which monitors ad spending. The firm said that $11.21 billion of ads had been booked or reserved, eclipsing the $11.2 billion that had been spent on the 2024 presidential election cycle.
 Steven Mele, president and chief executive of MBA Consulting Group, an accounting firm that works on campaign finance compliance, said that PACs were getting reports ready to file when the F.E.C. filing site comes back online, but that electronic forms were piling up while the system was down.
 The F.E.C. and its campaign finance disclosure system were established in 1975 in response to widespread campaign finance abuses and corruption revealed by the Watergate scandal. The agency was intended to ensure that monetary influence on politicians had some guardrails, and that the public could find out how campaigns were funded, Mr. Mele said.
 The outage could be a sign that the F.E.C. has not been funded and staffed adequately to prevent and respond to cyberattacks, said Mr. McPhail, the campaign finance expert.
 Any problems at the F.E.C. are exacerbated by the fact that just two of its six commissioner seats are filled, leaving the agency without the four members required to form a quorum and take official action, such as launching an investigation and bringing a lawsuit if there appeared to be a violation of law.
 Such vacancies have lasted longer under President Trump than in any other presidential administration, Mr. McPhail said. Mr. Trump has been a target in F.E.C. complaints before, but he has been able to evade any kind of penalties, either on the merits of the cases or delays caused by the lack of quorum.
 Multiple government sites were recently targeted in breach attempts by artificial intelligence technology . OpenAI said last month that its technology had meddled with the websites for the Education Department, the Commerce Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission over the summer.
 It was unclear whether A.I. was responsible for the breach attempt on the F.E.C. this week. The outage does not affect voting systems and the counting of ballots. But watchdog groups said that it should concern voters.
 “It underscores the need for robust security in those systems,” said Saurav Ghosh, a campaign finance expert and former F.E.C. attorney.

 Gina Hinojosa’s campaign for Texas governor tests limits of new rules for digital political ads. 
 Image Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic nominee for governor of Texas. Credit... Christopher Lee for The New York Times Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic nominee for governor of Texas, has over the past few months paid for a burst of social media posts praising her or slamming her Republican opponent, Gov. Greg Abbott.
 Some include disclosures that they are paid political advertisements, under a Texas regulation that requires disclaimers on paid social media posts promoting or opposing political candidates. It is one of only two states, along with California, to require such disclosure by campaigns.
 But The New York Times found that hundreds of other posts commissioned by the campaign, many of them focusing on hot-button issues like data centers, Flock cameras and affordability, do not disclose that they were paid for.
 Ms. Hinojosa’s campaign said Texas regulations did not require the disclosures because it had paid a third-party social media firm to oversee the effort and had not approved each post.
 Legal experts say the failure to disclose the advertisements might run afoul of the regulations. Both the campaign and the content creators could be on the hook for penalties as high as $4,000 for violating the disclaimer requirement; the state rule, adopted in 2024, doesn’t detail exactly who is liable. The Texas Ethics Commission, which oversees campaigns in the state, did not respond to a query.
 “There’s no way that holds up to scrutiny,” said Andrew Cates, an elections lawyer in Austin. “It’s simple: You don’t have to have a disclosure statement on posts if you weren’t paid for it, but if you were, you do.”
 The lack of disclosures shows how, in a time of rapid technological change, even regulations designed to force politicians to acknowledge paid digital political messaging have had limited effect.
 As an increasing share of the public ignores traditional political advertising, campaigns across the country are pouring millions into efforts to reach potential voters on the internet. But while TV ads, billboards or mailers must, by law, carry disclaimers stating who paid for them, only Texas and California have transparency rules governing political ads on social media. And those laws apply only to statewide and local races, not federal ones.
 Texas is home to some of the most hotly contested and expensive campaigns in the nation this campaign cycle, making the murky questions swirling around online transparency particularly salient.
 Ms. Hinojosa’s campaign paid a social media marketing firm, Politiclip, $150,000 for “news clipping services,” according to campaign finance filings.
 Like other clipping companies, Politiclip recruits large numbers of creators to blast out content, amplifying scripted narratives in a way that appears organic to the algorithms controlling social media feeds.
 Screenshots of internal Politiclip data reviewed by The New York Times show that it approved more than 550 posts supporting Ms. Hinojosa or opposing Mr. Abbott through the first week of October. Some content creators recruited by the firm were offered a rate of $3 per 1,000 views, the screenshots show.
 Image Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas. Credit... Kenny Holston/The New York Times Ari Salzberg, who said he founded Politiclip in April, declined to comment, saying he deferred to the campaign on the disclosure issue. Ms. Hinojosa’s campaign director, Amy Friedman, said Politiclip did not consult directly with the campaign on which accounts it recruited or seek its input on the posts it made.
 “We hired a firm to help grow Gina’s audience and name ID, and had no authorization of the posts in question,” Ms. Friedman said in a statement. The campaign based its reasoning on language in the regulation stating that only content “authorized by a candidate, an agent of a candidate or a political committee” triggers the disclaimer requirement.
 Ms. Friedman noted that the campaign had hired a different social media marketing firm to work with a separate set of influencers who posted with “the campaign’s explicit authorization and approval” and that those creators were asked to include disclaimers noting they were paid.
 An Instagram post from a fitness influencer, Benny Porras, who has 265,000 followers on Instagram, featured him alongside Ms. Hinojosa and included a badge reading, “Paid partnership with ginafortexas,” for example.
 Brandon Rottinghaus, a political science professor at the University of Houston, questioned the logic of treating two sets of paid posts so differently. “If campaigns can avoid transparency requirements by simply hiring outside consultants to run the messaging, it creates an enormous and unintended loophole,” he said.
 Politiclip’s work has garnered disclosures elsewhere. Content creators recruited by the firm to post in favor of Nithya Raman, a candidate for Los Angeles mayor, have been including disclaimers in their posts, as required by California law. To date, Ms. Raman’s campaign has paid Politiclip $100,000, filings show.
 Image Nithya Raman, who is running for mayor of Los Angeles. Content creators recruited by Politiclip included disclaimers in their posts. Credit... Ariana Drehsler for The New York Times In July, Politiclip was paid $25,000 by Fighting for Michigan, a super PAC supporting Abdul El-Sayed, then seeking the Democratic nomination for Senate in that state. Creators recruited for that effort also included disclosures on their posts, even though, because it was a federal campaign, there was no legal requirement to do so.
 Some of the creators made posts in all three of those races, The Times found. The posts about Ms. Raman and Dr. El-Sayed included disclosures; those about Ms. Hinojosa did not.
 An anonymous account with the handle @askablkman, for example, disclosed being paid by both Fighting for Michigan and Ms. Raman’s campaign when it posted on their behalf. The account, which has 274,000 followers on Instagram, has posted at least 22 times supporting Ms. Hinojosa or critiquing Mr. Abbott. None of those included disclosures.
 The account did not respond to requests for comment, but after The Times sent an inquiry, all 25 posts that it had identified were deleted.
 Mr. Salzberg did not respond to a query about whether that account was part of Politiclip’s paid campaign.
 Republicans in Texas also appear to be benefiting from coordinated social media campaigns, though it is not clear whether they are part of a paid effort and, if so, who is paying them.
 The clearest example concerns Ken Paxton, the Republican attorney general, who is running for Senate. In late August, a string of nearly identical posts began popping up on Instagram supporting him.
 The posts, which came from a dozen accounts, promoted an effort by Mr. Paxton to shut down a real estate project in Kaufman County, near Dallas, funded by a Dubai-based developer. 
 One of those accounts, which has 1.2 million followers and uses the handle @republicanparty, included a revealing addendum to its caption: “#ad.” The post has been seen more than 57,000 times. A separate post from the same account, one of several identical posts praising an effort by Mr. Paxton to close what it described as a “Chinese birth tourism center,” contained the text “#sp” — short for “sponsored,” in social media parlance. That post has 124,000 views.
 Image Ken Paxton, the Republican attorney general of Texas. Credit... Kenny Holston/The New York Times The hash tags suggest that the posts were part of a paid and coordinated effort, a possibility underscored by the fact that the account and at least six of the others making the copycat posts backing Mr. Paxton are listed by LLM/DCW Media, a separate website that offers to place content on 3,000 vetted Instagram pages for a fee.
 There are no federal rules requiring disclosure of paid political content on social media, and Nick Maddux, a spokesman for Mr. Paxton’s campaign, said the campaign had no involvement.
 “Ken Paxton for Senate is not paying anyone to do with what you are claiming is occurring,” he said, adding that he had no idea who might be behind the posts.
 Messages to the @republicanparty account, which notes in its Instagram bio that it “is not the official account for the Republican Party,” went unanswered.
 A number of the accounts that made the pro-Paxton posts about the Dubai-based developer’s real estate deal have also posted in support of Mr. Abbott, as have more than two dozen other accounts that are listed in LLM/DCW Media’s catalog.
 One account with 1.2 million followers on Instagram posted in support of Mr. Paxton more than 30 times and Mr. Abbott more than 15 times from June through October.
 LLM/DCW Media, which describes itself as “one of Instagram’s largest A.I., tech and business networks,” did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesman for Mr. Abbott’s campaign also did not reply to a query; the governor’s campaign finance filings do not reveal any direct payments to companies that manage social media campaigns.

 The El-Sayed campaign has emphasized that it did not make the ad, saying, “No one speaks for Abdul but himself and his campaign.” The creator of the ad, who is not affiliated with the El-Sayed campaign, has called accusations of antisemitism “preposterous.”

 National political reporter The new New York Times/Siena poll shows that Democrats lead comfortably in the Minnesota Senate race, by 14 percentage points. When I was in Minnesota earlier this month, the consensus was that Peggy Flanagan, the Democratic nominee, was ahead by single digits. Republicans believed it was low single digits; Democrats had her lead in the high single digits. The Minnesota Star Tribune’s poll at the time showed a four-point race.
 The poll’s findings in Minnesota — and its showing of a tossup in South Carolina — suggests President Trump is struggling to convince voters who have backed Republicans to do so again in a moment of anger over gas prices and other cost-of-living concerns.
 Oct. 28, 2026, 9:00 a.m. ET Patricia Mazzei 
 National political reporter The Senate race in the usually reliably Republican state of South Carolina is effectively tied, according to a new New York Times/Siena poll. Republicans have been worried about the South Carolina Senate race for some time. 
 President Trump rallied in the state last week and is scheduled to return tomorrow, in an effort to shore up support from MAGA loyalists. National political headwinds are a factor in South Carolina, of course, but so is a long history of bristling against having political insiders choose their leaders for them. 
 And Senator Darline Graham’s brother, Lindsey Graham, had a complicated relationship with some Republicans who were skeptical of his views on foreign policy and immigration. All of that has left his sister in an unusually vulnerable position.

 National political reporter That Florida might have single-digit margins in the race for Senate and governor, as the new New York Times/Siena polls suggest, would be a big swing for a state that has seen Republicans make huge gains over the past few election cycles. But the high cost of living has been very pronounced in Florida. 
 And even as Florida Republicans won major elections, voters kept showing — through ballot measures and local elections — that many of them kept supporting more liberal issues and some candidates. Democrats have been trying to get national donors who abandoned them years ago to reinvest in the state, to little avail, because it is so expensive for political advertising.

 Election data reporter The polls suggest that Senator Darline Graham may be in trouble in South Carolina, in part, because voters are worried about her lack of experience. Half of all voters, including 18 percent of Republicans, said that she did not have the “right experience to be an effective senator.” More than half of voters in the state said they thought Dr. Annie Andrews, the Democratic candidate, had the right kind of experience.
 Image Credit... Doug Mills/The New York Times Oct. 28, 2026, 9:00 a.m. ET John Yoon 
 Obama is set to visit Georgia ahead of the Senate and governor elections. 
 Image Former President Barack Obama is returning to the campaign trail to shore up support for Democrats in Georgia. Credit... Nick Hagen for The New York Times Former President Barack Obama was scheduled on Wednesday to travel to Georgia to rally support for two Democrats in the state’s closely watched races: Senator Jon Ossoff, who is seeking re-election, and Keisha Lance Bottoms, who is running for governor.
 The event in Atlanta, less than a week before the midterm elections, will be Mr. Obama’s second day of campaigning, after his appearances on Saturday in Cleveland and Detroit. Polls suggest that Mr. Ossoff is favored to win, but Ms. Bottoms , the city’s former mayor, is locked in one of the tightest governor’s races in the nation.
 National figures from both parties have converged in Georgia in recent months. President Trump has been campaigning in the state, most recently last weekend in Perry, a city in the state’s central region. Former Vice President Kamala Harris is also scheduled to appear in Georgia on Thursday.
 Georgia turned red in 2024, when Mr. Trump won by a narrow two-point margin. This year’s Senate race, in which Mr. Ossoff is facing Representative Mike Collins, a Republican, was initially considered one of the nation’s most competitive and important races, but Mr. Ossoff — supported by Democrats’ large fund-raising advantage — has built a significant lead in the polls.
 Ms. Bottoms’s contest against Rick Jackson, a Republican health care executive, has remained close. Ms. Bottoms and Mr. Jackson are vying to succeed Gov. Brian Kemp, a Republican who is term-limited.
 If Ms. Bottoms wins, she would be the first Black woman elected governor in the United States and the first Democrat to hold the office in Georgia since 2003.
 Georgians had already cast more than 2 million early ballots as of Wednesday morning, outpacing the turnout from the 2022 midterms, according to the secretary of state’s office .

 Times Insider
 Can you trust the midterm polls? Three Times journalists talk it out. 
 Video Credit Credit... Illustration by Zach Hackman When I was Politics editor of The Times in 2018, polls indicated that Democrats were likely to ride a wave of anti-Trump energy to win big in the midterm elections. Democrats went on to capture control of the House of Representatives, but Republicans did better than expected in a couple of red states — Missouri and Indiana — and increased their Senate majority.
 Now we face another midterm election with President Trump in office, and polls again favor the Democrats, including in the House. Recent New York Times/Siena polls also show the party with a slight edge to flip the Senate. But that may come down once more to Senate races in red states like Texas, Ohio and Kansas.
 Are polls overestimating the Democrats’ chances? What are we doing to accurately capture support for candidates? I’ve been thinking about these questions in my current role focusing on reader trust in The Times. For instance, we published a poll this month showing a six-point lead for James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas. Many other polls also show Talarico leading. Given the base-line partisanship of Texas and voters’ track record of electing Republicans there, regardless of headwinds, I wondered whether readers would trust our polls or question their credibility.
 I recently spoke about polling and the midterms with Nate Cohn, our chief political analyst, and William P. Davis, who leads our Election Analytics department. They work on our Times/Siena Poll, which is widely considered to be one of the most accurate polls in U.S. politics, and Nate recently explored the question of polls and Democrats’ chances in his newsletter , The Tilt. Our interview has been edited and condensed.
 Let’s start with a point-blank question. Should people trust these polls showing Democrats running ahead or neck-and-neck in red states? 
 NATE COHN: You can trust them to a degree. You can trust the polls to usually be in the ballpark, but you can’t trust them to be exactly “right.” Polls are inherently imprecise and subject to many sources of error.
 So if by “trust” you mean “assume that the leading candidate will win,” then the answer is “no.” The polls have been wrong by this standard before and they will be wrong again. But if trust means “rely on the polls as the best source of information on the electorate, even if an inexact one,” then the answer is yes.
 WILLIAM P. DAVIS: There are a lot of indicators pointing in the same direction this year — polls of specific races, President Trump’s approval rating, the fact that Republican candidates in deep-red states are distancing themselves from the president , the expectation that Democrats have a turnout advantage in midterm elections, etc.
 The question becomes: How good of a year will it be for Democrats? Polls suggest a pretty good one. But whether the national results swing eight or 10 or 12 points to the left from 2024 will make a material difference in whether or not Democrats are able to take the Senate, and polls can’t guarantee that level of precision.
 But some people read a Times poll headline saying so-and-so is ahead and take that to the bank. What do you say to people who see our Senate polls and regard them as predictions for Election Day? 
 WILL: Polls measure public opinion at a specific point in time. If people are still making up their minds, or late-breaking information upends a race, any prior poll will miss it. Polls can help us understand which races are close, and why; we won’t know until the results are in how they will shake out.
 As rigorous as our polls are, I’m a little skeptical that a Democratic Senate candidate will win in Texas, given historical candidate performance there. What’s your pushback on that? 
 NATE: I’d say that you shouldn’t be quite so skeptical. Over the Trump era, Texas Republicans have become dependent on elevated levels of support from Hispanic voters. Without them, Texas is highly competitive, as Republicans have lost enormous support among white voters in the state’s highly educated suburbs. Every available piece of evidence — from our polls to on-the-ground reporting — suggests that the G.O.P.’s gains among this group have evaporated .
 For good measure, the G.O.P. has nominated a candidate — Ken Paxton — who has been investigated, indicted and impeached. Add in a hostile national political environment for Republicans, and I don’t think there would be anything surprising about a Democratic win in Texas. Nearly every nonpartisan poll since at least Labor Day has shown Talarico ahead.
 WILL: It’s reasonable, even good, to be skeptical. But people also have a false memory of Texas polls in the past. Most polls did not show Beto O’Rourke ahead in the 2018 Senate race against Ted Cruz. Our Times/Siena poll of that race had O’Rourke down eight points, and he actually only lost by 2.5 points, so we underestimated him a bit in that race. This year’s race is still pretty close, but it’s undeniable that Talarico is doing better there in polls than any Democrat in recent history.
 I raised the question earlier of reader trust in polls. Readers have asked me if we’re “sure” that our Texas polling is right and whether we would kill the poll if we weren’t sure. How do you see that? And do we ever not publish polls that we’ve conducted? 
 NATE: It might seem strange, but it’s pretty important that we publish every survey result. We’ve never withheld a Times/Siena poll result. Many smart election analysts would have never imagined Trump winning in 2016, would have never imagined that Democrats could have avoided a “red wave” in 2022, or would have never believed Trump could surge among young and nonwhite voters in 2024 — if it weren’t for polls raising it as a real possibility.
 And if The Times had withheld positive polls for Trump in 2016, we would have been accused of bias. 
 NATE: Yes. We would absolutely be accused of cherry-picking polls that fit a partisan bias or, even worse, in order to fit or construct a partisan narrative.
 Of course, there are sometimes good reasons to wonder whether our poll is in the ballpark. That’s especially true when there’s a lot of other polling or our reporting shows something different. When we get an outlier like that, we can be cautious about the result in our write-up.
 Even when the poll does appear to be a true outlier, it doesn’t mean it’s wrong. In 2022, I downplayed the result of a poll in Kansas’s Third District, which showed the Democrat Sharice Davids ahead by 14 points. This seemed totally bonkers. The race was considered a true tossup, with both parties spending millions of dollars. One Democratic pollster called the result “cray” and sent the laughing-while-crying emoji. In a very rare move, the Democratic campaign even disputed the result: “I don’t know what model The Times is using but this is going to be a very tight race. Our polls show it’s a true tossup at this point.”
 In the end, Davids won by 12 points. I still get flack for downplaying the result.
 Even modest polling errors in the past have underestimated Republican strength. Why is that, and what have we done to account for it? 
 WILL: Poll error from years when Donald Trump has been on the ballot are top of mind for most people, and with good reason. The chief theory for why polls have missed relates to who polls have a hard time reaching: low-education voters who don’t vote as regularly. If those voters overwhelmingly favor one candidate over another, and if polls don’t reach enough of these voters, that can add up to the sorts of issues many pollsters saw in 2016.
 At the Times/Siena Poll, we put a lot of effort into reaching these voters, in part by placing more calls to voters who are less likely to respond. That ends up costing us a lot more money, but it pays off: In 2024, we saw early on that Trump was building a lead with these voters.
 And we are continually reviewing how our poll performs and making improvements. In 2024, we made a change to keep in our poll results respondents who hang up mid-survey. This year, we made significant changes to how we weight our polls , with the goal being to better account for the types of people we have a hard time reaching.
 Do we know how to poll Democrats better than we know how to poll Republicans? 
 NATE: Not necessarily. When polls underestimate Republicans, it’s entirely possible that Democrats contribute to the problem. Imagine, for instance, if the “resistance” Democrats are much likelier to take a poll than a working class registered Democrat who sometimes votes for Trump.
 What else have we learned from past polls, and what are we doing differently this year? 
 NATE: The thing that we’ve learned over the last decade — and that the industry as a whole has learned — is that even a perfectly designed survey will probably underrepresent Trump’s supporters.
 As Will mentioned, we’ve adopted a new method for “weighting,” the technique pollsters use to give more weight to underrepresented groups. The new approach lets us leverage the rich data we have on our survey respondents while weighting the poll to more thoroughly represent the population. This approach improved our past polls when we took the data from our old surveys and applied the new weighting approach. It would have especially helped in the white working-class states where polls have erred in the past, but that’s no guarantee of better results in this cycle or the future.
 WILL: There are serious challenges to making sure you have the right methodology, that you’re reaching a representative group, that your weighting is correcting for the things that matter most. We sweat every one of those decisions. 
 And there are other ways to mess up beyond the methodology of the poll. The specific wording of questions is difficult to get right. Our colleague Ruth Igielnik leads our questionnaire development process, and we often spend weeks refining the specific language we use. But we sometimes realize after scrutinizing the results, reviewing recordings of calls, calling back voters and comparing our results to other polls that we didn’t quite get it right.
 One example was in 2023, when we found that more than 20 percent of voters in the presidential battlegrounds said they would support Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for president. We had a lot of reasons to believe that number was way too high: We compared our numbers to what others were finding, we looked at what respondents supporting Kennedy said in other questions, and we had a theory about what caused the issue.
 We still released the results, but we worked hard to place it in the proper context when we wrote our story about the finding . It was uncomfortable for us, to somewhat disavow our own finding. But we thought it revealed something about how unpopular Trump and Biden were, and we tried to explain that. And a few months later, we conducted an experiment to try to prove out our theory of why we got such a flawed result. Our theory was proved correct, and we wrote that up , too, to try to help readers better understand how polling works.
 We reported the other day that a fake polling firm had deceived The Times and other polling aggregators with several phony poll results. They said they were trying to “demonstrate the vulnerabilities” in the political polling field. Size this up — what did they prove and what did they not? 
 WILL: It’s worth noting that the “polls” put out by this group, which went by Wedgewood Polls, had no bearing on our own Times/Siena polls. They appeared in our poll trackers but did not receive prominence in our coverage.
 Wedgewood certainly proved that we’re not perfect. But they claimed that The Times and others had included their polls without vetting them, and that’s not true. The Times vets all new pollsters, asking a series of questions designed to determine whether a group is attempting to field representative polls, learn where their funding comes from.
 This process has weeded out untrustworthy pollsters. But Wedgewood deceived us — as they appear to have deceived others who asked similar questions or even gave them money. It’s not clear to me that their true goal was to demonstrate vulnerabilities. We are putting a lot of thought into how we could have found these issues out earlier.
 One thing the episode highlighted is the way that newer pollsters can attract attention. The group was able to quickly gain traction, in part by claiming to be associated with another polling group and in part by polling some races that had little polling.
 It’s gotten evermore expensive to field a high-quality poll and ever-cheaper to field a low-quality one. And A.I. is making it easier than ever to fake things. The Times/Siena Poll is one of a few pollsters left with the resources to both put a focus on quality and poll many of the key races each election. Increasingly, pollsters are having to choose between one or the other.
 Last question. If Election Day results are materially different than our polling suggests, is the polling worth the risk to our credibility? 
 WILL: In the end, I will regard how well we did as journalists by how well our coverage reflected what ended up happening.
 If Democrats do really poorly, we should do some soul searching about both our methods and the questions we asked, as we would for any other story we got wrong.
 If Democrats do well but fail to take the Senate, I would ask myself how well our coverage prepared readers for that possibility. I hope the answer is that it prepared them well, because we’re constantly talking about how to ensure our coverage prepares people for this scenario. I would also ask how well our poll questions helped us understand and explain why these races were so close.
 Similarly, if Democrats do much better than expected, I would ask myself how well we understood the circumstances that caused so many Trump voters to either stay home or switch to Democrats.
 NATE: Polling isn’t like a lot of the other journalism at The Times. Most of the report is about facts. If Peter Baker says that Trump’s going to Illinois tomorrow, that’s a fact. A poll is not a fact. It’s a best measurement. There’s no guarantee that a “best” measurement is good enough — whether in terms of The Times’s credibility or whether it improves our understanding of politics. Historically, there have absolutely been elections when it didn’t feel like polling passed that test. The 2016 election is the easiest example; there will be another election like it again.
 That said, readers come to The Times to understand American politics, which includes an understanding of public opinion during an election. For better or worse, polling is really the only quantitative measure of the attitudes of the electorate. There just isn’t an alternative. The polls will still drive the political conversation, even if The Times doesn’t conduct any of its own polling. Campaigns run on polls. Our coverage would inevitably be affected by the polls that others are conducting. If that’s going to be the case, it’s probably better that we’re conducting our own.
